notes:
These are my notes on Mark 12:1–22, verse by verse. Before you use them, you should know about some gaps:

- **Searches I didn't get to:** I didn't reach any Lutheran, Wesleyan or Orthodox source, the NET Bible notes on netbible.org (I only saw them quoted on Precept Austin), or any prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this passage.
- **Pages I only saw in part:** I read Enduring Word, Bible Hub, StudyLight and Precept Austin mostly through search excerpts and partial pages. I didn't read the full Gill, Ellicott or Pulpit notes. Bible Hub labels its notes on v. 1 as Ellicott's, but on v. 18 it only points to his Matthew notes. So the v. 18 and v. 22 notes I quote there aren't clearly labelled, and I haven't named an author for them.
- **Where traditions differ:** The pages I read didn't show clear Protestant denominational splits. Where I found real disagreement, I've marked it **[Differing view]**.

---

**v. 1**
- The parable picks up Isaiah's vineyard song (Isa 5). The man in the parable represents God, the vineyard is Israel (Psalms 80:8-19; Jeremiah 2:21), and the tenants are Israel's leaders. (Constable) https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/mark-12.html
- MacLaren says we shouldn't read special meanings into the wall, winepress and tower. Their point is that God had given Israel everything it needed for fruitful service. He also thinks the vineyard here stands less for the nation and more for Israel's religious privileges and institutions. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/12-1.htm
- Precept Austin cites Barton: tenant estates with absentee owners were common in Galilee, so the setting was familiar. The parable indirectly answers the leaders' question about Jesus' authority. https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-12-commentary
- MacLaren on the owner going away: in the long years without miracles, God was as near as before, but He seemed far off. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/12-1.htm
- Contending for the Faith warns that "far country" can mislead. The parable implies the owner hasn't gone far away or forgotten his tenants. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ctf/mark-12.html

**v. 2**
- The harvest time stands for the time when God expected to obtain some reward for His investment in Israel. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/mark-12.html
- Background: vines usually took at least five years to produce commercially, and the owner expected his share. https://bible.org/seriespage/mark-12
- Precept Austin explains that the owner had to receive some produce to keep his legal rights to the land. That is why the tenants refused to pay, and why the owner kept sending agents. https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-12-commentary

**v. 3**
- The NET note (quoted on Precept Austin) says the beating pictures the nation's rejection of the prophets. The servants coming back empty-handed suggests the vineyard, and so Israel, was producing no fruit. https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-12-commentary
- The Light of Israel commentary, citing Evans, says ancient papyri show such tenants were often groups of large, powerful commercial farmers, which explains why rent was hard to collect. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/12-12.html

**v. 4**
- The tenants grow more violent. Precept Austin points to Hebrews 11:36–38 and to prophets who were beaten (Jeremiah) and stoned (2 Chron 24:21). https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-12-commentary

**v. 5**
- The servants are the prophets. The main point of the parable is the wicked treatment Israel's leaders had given the servants whom God had sent to them. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/mark-12.html
- Precept Austin, quoting Wiersbe on Luke's version, sees sin getting worse over time: the tenants start with beatings and end as murderers. Likewise the leaders allowed John's death, demanded Jesus' death, and then stoned Stephen themselves. https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-12-commentary
- The Bridgeway commentary traces the persecuted messengers from the Old Testament prophets to John the Baptist. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/12-12.html

**v. 6**
- MacLaren says that by calling himself the Son, Jesus sets himself apart from the prophets, who were only servants. His Sonship is not just another word for being Messiah; it was true long before Bethlehem. He also reads the owner's words "They will respect my son" as a disappointed hope, which shows that people can resist God's purpose. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/12-1.htm
- Precept Austin argues that the parable answers the question about Jesus' authority (Mark 11:27–33). His authority rests on his being the "beloved son." https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-12-commentary

**v. 7**
- Contending for the Faith stresses that this was planned, not impulsive: it was premeditated murder. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ctf/mark-12.html
- Bible.org connects "the inheritance will be ours" to a Jewish law allowing ownerless property to be claimed by whoever possessed it. It reflects mankind's fallen attitude of "more and more for me at any cost." Humanity wants to be its own god (cf. Genesis 3). https://bible.org/seriespage/mark-12
- MacLaren doesn't think the rulers had openly admitted Jesus was Messiah. He thinks Jesus was exposing motives they hadn't admitted even to themselves. He quotes Augustine: they killed him to gain possession, and by killing him they lost it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/12-1.htm

**v. 8**
- Mark puts the killing before the throwing out (Matthew and Luke reverse the order). Constable says Mark's order shows that the murder was also an act of rejection. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/mark-12.html
- Throwing the body over the wall symbolises Jesus being shut out of Israel. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/12-1.htm
- Bible.org: leaving the body unburied shows complete contempt for the owner and his son. https://bible.org/seriespage/mark-12

**v. 9**
- Guzik: the leaders rejected messenger after messenger and finally the Son, so their day of reckoning would come. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-12/
- Bible Hub's summary sees the coming judgment as pointing ahead to Jerusalem's fall in AD 70 and to the gospel going to the Gentiles. https://biblehub.com/mark/12.htm
- Precept Austin, quoting Got Questions, compares this to Nathan's question to David: Jesus makes the leaders pronounce their own sentence. https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-12-commentary
- **[Differing view: who are "those tenants"?]** James Edwards (quoted on Precept Austin) says the owner punishes the tenants, not the vineyard, so the parable cannot be interpreted as a blanket judgment on the Jewish people, but rather on their leaders, particularly the Sanhedrin. He adds that the hero is the owner, not the tenants, so the parable can't be read as backing a popular uprising against oppressive landlords. https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-12-commentary
- MacLaren disagrees in part. Because Matthew speaks of the vineyard going to another nation, he thinks the whole nation is included among the tenants, though the rulers are addressed first. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/12-1.htm
- The Jamieson-Fausset-Brown (JFB) heading on the same page reads the parable more broadly still, as foretelling God's rejection of the Jews and the calling of the Gentiles. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/12-1.htm

**v. 10**
- Bible.org notes that in rabbinic writing "builders" meant the scribes. The builders are condemned for missing the main truth, that Jesus is the promised Messiah. https://bible.org/seriespage/mark-12
- Calvin reads Psalm 118:22 as Jesus saying Scripture itself predicted that the rulers would oppose him. He draws two comforts from it: God warned us in advance about opposition, and God's power will win in setting up Christ's kingdom. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/mark/12.htm
- MacLaren: the builders are the same people as the vine-dressers. In the same breath Jesus predicts his death and his exaltation. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/12-1.htm

**v. 11**
- Matthew Henry: exalting Christ is the Lord's doing. So is exalting him in our hearts, and when that happens it is marvellous in our eyes. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/12-1.htm
- David Garland (quoted on Precept Austin) says the quotation presents Jesus' condemnation of the temple as God's own work. Those with eyes to see find it marvellous. https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-12-commentary

**v. 12**
- Guzik: the leaders were convicted, but they responded by rejecting rather than receiving. They plotted murder instead of repenting. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-12/
- Contending for the Faith, citing Ellicott: unable to act in public, they withdrew and fell back on scheming and treachery. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/12-12.html
- Ligonier applies the passage to the heavy accountability of those who lead God's people. When God's people fail to bear fruit, it is linked to their leaders failing to teach and discipline them. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/parable-of-tenants

**v. 13**
- Guzik: public opinion stopped the leaders from seizing Jesus, so they tried to turn the crowd against him. The Pharisees and Herodians were former enemies, united only by opposing him (compare Mark 3:6). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-12/

**v. 14**
- Guzik: Jesus ignored flattery from enemies who wanted to harm him. The trap was this: saying "pay" would seem to deny God's rule over Israel and lose the crowd, while saying "don't pay" would mark him as a revolutionary against Rome. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-12/
- Bible.org puts it the same way: answering yes would offend the zealots, and answering no would get him arrested by Rome. https://bible.org/seriespage/mark-12
- Calvin finds in their flattering words a real description of a faithful teacher: one who teaches God's way rather than human inventions, without being corrupted by ambition or greed. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/mark/12.htm
- Catholic view: the questioners didn't want a conversation or a debate; they just wanted to get Jesus into trouble. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/render-unto

**v. 15**
- Calvin says we need Christ to give us discernment, because wicked people use the same traps today. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/mark/12.htm
- Guzik: as Jesus held the coin, he knew Caesar's government would soon crucify him, yet he still told them to pay. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-12/

**v. 16**
- Bible.org on the coin: the front read "Tiberius Caesar Augustus, son of the Divine Augustus." On the back of the coin was a picture of Tiberius seated on a throne and the inscription "Highest Priest." https://bible.org/seriespage/mark-12
- Bible Odyssey (modern scholarship) describes the same kind of coin. It has the emperor's image and titles, including "Pontifex Maximus," with a female figure shown as the goddess Pax. https://www.bibleodyssey.org/articles/render-unto-caesar/
- Bible Hub: by answering "Caesar's," the questioners themselves admit Caesar's authority, so they can't accuse Jesus of sedition. The word "image" also recalls humans made in God's image (Gen 1:27). https://biblehub.com/mark/12-16.htm
- Sproul: under Roman law, Caesar's image and name on the coin showed he owned it. https://learn.ligonier.org/sermons/mark-god-and-caesar

**v. 17**
- Common evangelical reading (Guzik): pay your taxes and submit to government, as long as it doesn't interfere with serving God (Rom 13:6–7). The coin bears Caesar's image, and we bear God's, so we give ourselves to God. When the state demands what belongs to God alone, we must obey God first. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-12/
- Early church: Tertullian, quoted on Bible Hub, gave the same reading: give Caesar the coin with his image, and give God yourself, stamped with God's image. https://biblehub.com/mark/12-17.htm
- Bible.org notes that "render" may mean giving back what already belongs to someone. https://bible.org/seriespage/mark-12
- Reformed (Calvin): those who overturn political order rebel against God. But if rulers claim any part of God's authority, we obey them only as far as we can without offending God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/mark/12.htm
- Reformed (Sproul): even unjust taxes must be paid. Caesar is owed taxes, not worship, which is why early Christians died rather than worship the emperor. https://learn.ligonier.org/sermons/render-unto-caesar
- Chadwick (Expositor's Bible) calls the saying a charter protecting the state from power-hungry churchmen. He also says the parallel implies God claims everything we have and are. https://ccel.org/ccel/chadwick/mark/mark.xiv.ii.html
- Catholic: the coin bears Caesar's image, and human beings, Caesar included, bear God's. So Caesar, and the state itself, belong to God. Citizens are bound in conscience to refuse civil orders that go against the moral order or the Gospel. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/when-is-it-okay-to-disobey
- Another Catholic writer warns against using the verse to split life into sealed compartments (politics here, "religion" there). He calls that deism, not Christianity. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/render-unto
- Modern use: Bible Odyssey notes that the verse is now often quoted to argue for separating church and state. It is read as meaning that government and economics should be kept apart from religion. https://www.bibleodyssey.org/articles/render-unto-caesar/
- "They marveled": Guzik notes they later twisted the answer into a false charge (Luke 23:2). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-12/

**v. 18**
- Guzik: the Sadducees did not believe in immortality, spirits or angels. Their question was meant to make resurrection look absurd. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-12/
- Chuck Smith adds that the high priest at this time was always a Sadducee. They were materialists who had taken control of the religious system. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/12-22.html
- Bible Hub: the scenario was meant to mock the doctrine of resurrection, not to seek the truth. https://biblehub.com/mark/12-18.htm

**v. 19**
- MacArthur (gty.org) notes they are quoting Deuteronomy 25:5, the levirate law ("levir" means brother-in-law). https://www.gty.org/sermons/41-62/biblical-ignorance-in-high-places
- A commentator on StudyLight (no author named in the excerpt) points out that their quotation leaves out one condition of the law: that the brothers lived together. A child born of the levirate marriage counted as the first husband's child. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/12-18.html
- Bridgeway describes the brother's role as a temporary marriage for the purpose of producing an heir. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/12-22.html

**vv. 20–21**
- Another StudyLight comment (again no author named) suggests that by citing this law, the Sadducees were implying Moses did not believe in resurrection. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/12-20.html
- Coffman calls the story contrived. It was technically possible, and Jesus answered it anyway. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/12-20.html

**v. 22**
- Ligonier calls the scenario implausible but an effective way to cast doubt on resurrection. Jesus traces the Sadducees' error to not knowing the Scriptures (v. 24). https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/sadducees-ask-about-marriage
- Coffman says it isn't clear why seven brothers would be a bigger problem than two. It was simply their way of mocking the resurrection. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/12-22.html
- An older commentary excerpted on Bible Hub (author not clear on the page) thinks such a case may really have happened. https://biblehub.com/mark/12-18.htm
- Guzik calls the question absurd. An absurd question isn't less absurd because it is put to God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-12/
